chunks: Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Hassan, from Muhammad ibn Ali, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu Hamza, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:
Fever for a night equates to worship for a year, and fever for two nights equates to worship for two years, and fever for three (nights) equates to worship for seventy years.

He (the narrator) said: I said, 'What if he does not reach seventy years (of age)?' He said: 'Then it is for his mother and his father.' I said, 'What if they both do not reach (that)?' He said: 'Then it is for his relatives.' I said, 'What if his relatives do not reach (that)?' He said: 'Then it is for his neighbours.'

key_terms.تَعْدِلُ: equates to, equals in divine reward
key_terms.حُمَّى: fever — used metaphorically as a form of involuntary worship

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Baqir say about the spiritual reward of fever?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) teaches that illness — specifically fever — carries immense spiritual reward that is credited not only to the sick person but overflows to benefit their family, relatives, and neighbours. This hadith reflects the Shia theological perspective that suffering endured with patience is a form of worship, and that divine mercy is so expansive it extends to those close to the patient. The progressive structure — parents, then relatives, then neighbours — illustrates the Islamic concept of concentric circles of social responsibility.
